body.text: Move over the "killing season". Enter, the hiring season.
For the second year in a row, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has used the end of the federal parliament sitting calendar to announce a new star recruit to her ranks.
In one fell swoop she has again delivered a blow to an Opposition leader still finding their feet and built a sense of momentum behind her party at a critical time.

The defection of South Australian Senator Leah Blyth from the Liberal Party to One Nation has interrupted what was shaping up to be a relatively upbeat end to an otherwise miserable political year for the Coalition.
The sight of tinsel adorning the parliamentary offices of MPs has historically signalled the most dangerous time of the year for a political leader under pressure.

It is the final opportunity for their colleagues to collectively decide whether this is the person they want leading them into the new year, or if their political fortunes might be better served by a reset.
But with Blyth following in the footsteps of Barnaby Joyce almost a year to the day, Hanson is establishing something of a tradition of her own.

A few months ago, it would have been fair to say the spectre of the so-called "killing season" loomed large over Opposition leader Angus Taylor, with some colleagues privately questioning whether the Coalition was capable of recovering under his leadership.
But Taylor, who just last week surpassed Sussan Ley's time in the top job, ultimately came into this sitting period with a spring in his step.
The Coalition had begun to climb in the polls, and in one recent result Taylor actually came out ahead of Anthony Albanese as preferred prime minister on a two-party preferred basis.
Oh, what a difference a few days can make.
Having spent much of the year trying to stem the flow of conservative votes to One Nation, Taylor reaches Christmas losing a member of his own party room to his rival.

Hanson played her part with a flair for the dramatic — giving the public a bit of a "forward sizzle" overnight on Wednesday when she posted a video online of herself cooking a steak in a sandwich press.
An increasingly narrow church
But sharing dubious culinary choices on the respective eves of their defection to One Nation is about where the similarities between Blyth and Joyce end.

A year ago, Joyce largely owned the fact that personal grievances — including being denied a spot on the frontbench and the influence he wanted in the Coalition party room — were motivating factors in his departure.
Blyth has sought to frame her defection as a matter of values, despite struggling to identify a substantive policy decision that drove her out of the Liberal party room.
Her Liberal colleagues, blindsided by the news, have been quick to characterise the move as one of political self-interest.
Such was the secrecy around Blyth's deliberations, even her own staff reportedly learned of the defection while at the pub late last night for a Christmas party.
Having entered parliament via a casual vacancy less than two years ago, Blyth's prospects of securing preselection to contest the election were, according to most Liberals, non-existent.
Her political fortunes have been inextricably linked to the factional warfare that has come to characterise the South Australian Liberal Party.
Senator Alex Antic's efforts to consolidate control of the state division, culminating in his ascension to the presidency, have coincided with the deterioration in his relationship with Blyth.
Blyth herself has said she no longer felt safe in the Liberal Party, noting security guards were hired to accompany her to a state annual general meeting in September.
Her claim the party had alienated her was arguably far more compelling than the case she ultimately put forward.
Instead, Blyth said she was disappointed that, having abandoned its commitment to net zero, the Coalition had compromised by opting to remain in the Paris Agreement.
Given the Coalition's broader shift on climate policy, the distinction hardly amounts to a seismic ideological divide between her old party and her new one.

Pressed to identify another instance in which she felt her values had been compromised, Blyth cited the lack of debate over legislation that gives the defence minister sweeping powers to designate areas for defence purposes.
But One Nation, as it was pointed out to her, voted for that bill too.
It didn't help when she later admitted to News24: "I am not completely across all of the different policy positions that One Nation have."
What emerged more clearly from Blyth's explanation was her frustration at having to accommodate the views of moderates within the Liberal party room — even when the conservative majority prevailed.
The Liberal Party has long prided itself as a "broad church" that facilitates internal debate in a way the strict caucus solidarity rules governing the Labor Party often do not.
Hanson's summer spoils

Even if Blyth's decision wasn't driven by her own preselection fortunes, her departure speaks to a broader challenge sparked by the polarisation of politics, where few are willing to even hear out different views.
Whatever the motivations of her latest recruit, the defection is an enormous political win for Hanson.

One Nation's electoral appeal is about to be tested in Victoria, where the party's prospects of picking up seats in the upper house appear more promising than its chances of making inroads in the lower house.
Hanson hasn't played a prominent role in the Victorian election, but here she is again seizing national headlines and causing headaches for Taylor.

For the second year running, she has ensured Coalition MPs will head into the summer break contemplating the threat One Nation poses not just to their electoral prospects, but to the cohesion of their own ranks.
But what is less clear is whether the politicians she is recruiting stand to gain as much from the arrangement as she does.
In singing Blyth's praises, Hanson claimed Joyce had achieved more in his 12 months with One Nation than he had during his time in the Nationals.
That made for an awkward exchange when it was pointed out to Joyce that he had, on multiple occasions, risen to the rank of deputy prime minister during his tenure with the Coalition.
Joyce sought to emphasise what lay ahead of him, rather than dwell on his past achievements.
But for all the airtime afforded to Joyce since his defection, it is difficult to mount an argument that he wields more influence now than he once did.
Perhaps there is a cautionary tale in that for any other Coalition MPs contemplating a switch.
There is a difference between having a louder voice in Australian politics and having the power to do something with it.
For now, at least, the biggest beneficiary of the hiring season is Hanson herself.
